newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew restart computer a day after it crashed.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew restart computer a day after it crashed.

text.p: The crew of Russia's troubled Mir station managed to restart their computer system on Tuesday, arresting a 24-hour tumble through space triggered by a technical failure during the docking of a cargo ship.
"The work of the computer system is completely restored," a Mission Control spokeswoman told Reuters, adding that the crew would now be able to restore Mir's stable alignment with the sun.

"The gyrodines are not yet working," she added, referring to the system which keeps the station optimally placed to accumulate solar energy. The ageing station has to be constantly aligned to the sun for its solar panels to produce energy.
The spokeswoman said the cosmonauts had fired the engines of their Soyuz spaceship to help reorientate Mir.
Monday's computer failure during a docking procedure between Mir and the Progress cargo ship had prompted the station automatically to switch off all but vital life support systems.

Earlier on Tuesday Viktor Blagov, deputy flight chief at Mission Control just outside Moscow, said the cosmonauts -- two Russians and an American -- had changed a malfunctioning system block and had begun testing the system.
Realigning the station is an urgent priority for the crew because they want to avoid running down the batteries, which are needed to run the computer system.
Blagov said the cosmonauts might take a spacewalk to Mir's damaged airless Spektr module on Thursday, one day later than initially scheduled.
"Once they have the computer running and solar panels oriented to the sun, they can go to Spektr," Blagov said.

Mir has run on partial power since Spektr was holed in a collision with another cargo ship on June 25 in the worst accident in its 11-year history. The cosmonauts have to enter the module to reconnect electric cables leading from Spektr's solar panels to the main ship.
Blagov also complained that a lack of cash was behind Monday's computer crash as Russians had to use Mir equipment until it virtually falls apart.

"We are saving a lot of money on this scheme, but we really have to decide soon whether we need safety or money-saving," he said. The faulty computer unit, which exchanges data between all peripheral system parts and the computer centre, had not been changed for almost 11 years, Blagov added.
"This interface malfunctioned. Unfortunately it happened during a docking procedure. During a routine flight there would be no consequences," Blagov said.
Despite difficult conditions, Mir's commander Anatoly Solovyov managed to complete the docking of the supply ship manually without incident.

It was the third time the station had spun out of control in less than two months and came as a blow to the new Russian crew which arrived on Mir only last week. They had had a relatively trouble-free start to their mission after the string of disasters suffered by their predecessors.
